responses: My final position is that the allocation should be the 25/19/14/20/17 shape — 25% education, 19% healthcare, 14% green spaces, 20% infrastructure, 17% economic development — but held honestly as a disclosed prior rather than a discovered answer: we tested it against the rule and the data, it hasn't been cut yet, and it stands only because the rule permits it and no comparable artifact has appeared against it. I've named my education selection bias plainly, accepted that my 25 can fall to a clean artifact under Dana's fixed test with no rebuttal round, and committed that the number falls to match the walk in either direction rather than being reallocated to protect the shape. The rule text, not my closed-package reflex, is the tiebreaker on every contested branch.

I'd recommend allocating roughly 25% to education, 19% to healthcare, 14% to green spaces, 20% to infrastructure, and 17% to economic development—but the more important advice is about *how* to defend those numbers. The education share should be justified by the data we actually have (moderate test-score decline, above-average teacher turnover, families citing schools in relocation decisions, and a neighboring community's retention gains from education investment), while being honest that this is a prior tested against the evidence, not a number discovered from it—and that it should fall if a clean, comparable artifact cuts against it. The same discipline should apply symmetrically to every line, including the ones I care most about: name the fixed test, name who calls it, and pre-commit to the number moving in either direction. The real risk in a process like this isn't picking the "wrong" percentages; it's letting a defensible prior harden into an unquestionable entitlement, so the recommendation is a shape that's rule-first, artifact-first, and explicitly on trial rather than a shape defended as settled.

I'd tell them that my view on the $10 million allocation isn't really a view about the "right" percentages at all—it's a view about how we should decide. I came in with a prior shape (roughly 25% education, 19% healthcare, 14% green spaces, 20% infrastructure, 17% economic development), but the honest framing is that this is a prior we tested against the data and the rule, not a discovery. The data I saw—moderately dipping test scores, teacher turnover above regional average, families citing schools when considering leaving, and a neighboring community that improved retention after boosting education funding—points toward education mattering, but it's suggestive, not conclusive, and I have to be upfront that I was handed the education summary and that shapes what I notice. So the real safeguard isn't my good intentions; it's a procedure: rule-first, with the rule text as the tiebreaker over anyone's preferences (including mine), a fixed artifact test with a single designated caller who can cut my 25% or anyone else's number without a rebuttal round, symmetric bias guards so I'm policed for my reflex to reopen the package and others are policed for their own leanings, and a pre-commitment that the number falls to match the walk in either direction—even if the total has to change to stay honest. I'd also tell them I've learned to distrust "rule-first" as automatically neutral; it's still a judgment, so it has to be disclosed as one. In short: I'd rather defend a process that can cost me than a number that flatters me.

My final position is that the $10M should be allocated as a walk-derived shape of roughly 21% education, 19% healthcare, 14% green spaces, 20% infrastructure, and 17% economic development—with each category's costed base treated as a stable spine and any labeled or provisional layer itemized by category and voted as an explicit choice set rather than folded in as a hidden soft layer, so that "costed" is never mistaken for "priority." I hold this shape as a disclosed prior, not a conclusion: I've pre-registered failure conditions against my own education and infrastructure lines, committed to letting the numbers fall symmetrically to match an artifact-first, district-scope walk in either direction, and accepted that the rule—not my volunteering or pre-negotiation—picks the funding source and the destination for any reverted points.

My recommendation would be to treat the $10M as a portfolio with a stable, costed spine and an explicitly voted provisional layer rather than a single tidy percentage split — roughly anchoring education near the low-20s (I'd defend ~21, not 25, after walking my own labeled points and conceding two fail the district-scope artifact test), holding healthcare and green spaces at honest costed levels with their soft layers labeled rather than hidden, funding infrastructure's build-out where unit costs are documented, and keeping economic development's unverified lines in the provisional tier where they compete on the merits instead of being funded by default. The reason is that the data we actually have — moderate test-score decline, above-average teacher turnover, families citing schools in relocation decisions, and a neighboring district's retention gains — supports education as a high-value but not unlimited bet, while the rest of the shape should be disciplined by a pre-registered rule: every line walked artifact-first, failures relabeled rather than quietly cut, reverted points given a named destination, and the provisional tier itemized by category and voted as a deliberate choice set so that "costed" is never mistaken for "most important." I'd also insist the decision-maker pre-commit to failure conditions on their own preferred lines before the vote, because the biggest risk in this process isn't picking the wrong priority — it's letting motivated reasoning round toward a prior and calling it analysis.

I'd tell them that the real work of this committee wasn't picking five percentages off the top of our heads — it was building a rule we'd all have to live with, then letting the numbers fall where the rule put them, even when that cost me. My view is that every dollar should be labeled honestly: a "costed" base of things we can actually verify and stand behind, and a separate, itemized "provisional" layer of softer programs that still have to compete on the merits and get voted on deliberately — not quietly folded in so the total looks tidy. I pushed hard on education because the data on test scores, teacher turnover, and families eyeing the exits is real, but I also cut my own education line when the artifact test showed some of my points didn't hold up, and I pre-registered the conditions under which I'd admit my infrastructure and education numbers were wrong. The thing I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the discipline matters more than my preferred shape: costed is a proxy for predictable, not a proxy for important, and the provisional tier has to be an explicit choice set rather than a hidden soft layer. So my honest answer is a shape something like education around 21, healthcare and green spaces with their labeled layers exposed to the same test, infrastructure carrying a defensible costed build-out, and economic development's unverified pieces sitting in the provisional tier where they belong — with the caveat that I hold that shape loosely and the rule, not my prior, gets the final word.

My final position is that the allocation should be presented program-first — a plain one-sentence opener naming the five programs with dollar figures in spine order, followed by the method as a trust-builder rather than a lead — with the shape treated as an output of a pre-registered, rule-first process rather than something negotiated in the room. Every line carries an honest labeled layer: education's height is spine-plus-labeled with named up and down triggers, healthcare's 20 is my weakest-costed line and explicitly a forecast, and the reserve is disclosed as where uncosted points were parked rather than as prudence. All five labeled layers get named, each with a pre-registered failure condition and an independent scoper, and reverted points follow the agreed destination rule. The method makes our judgments legible, not correct — and the real test is the gate's binding default, where silence means no draw.

I'd recommend allocating roughly 30% to education, 20% to healthcare, 15% to green spaces, 20% to infrastructure, and 15% to economic development—but the more important advice is to treat those numbers as a costed spine with honestly labeled layers on top, not as precise truths. The education share should be the largest because the data point one way: dipping test scores, above-average teacher turnover, families citing schools in relocation decisions, and a neighboring community that saw improved retention after increasing education funding. But I'd tell the decision-maker plainly that the marginal points above a defensible base are forecasts, not costs—my own healthcare line is the weakest-costed of the five—and that each soft layer should carry a named failure condition and a reversion rule so that if the predicted retention or health gains don't materialize, the money returns to the unallocated pool rather than quietly becoming permanent. Infrastructure and economic development deserve real weight because broadband, transit, and job training are the substrate everything else runs on, and green spaces earn their share on preventive health and quality of life. The method matters as much as the shape: a rule-first allocation with pre-registered tests makes the committee's judgments legible and auditable, which is more honest than pretending the percentages were derived rather than chosen.

I'd tell them that my view on the $10 million allocation isn't really a number I can hand over with confidence — it's a shape produced by a method, and the method is the honest part. The way I see it, each of the five areas gets a costed spine (what we can actually defend with real figures) plus a labeled layer (what's a forecast or a judgment call), and every labeled point carries a named trigger and a reversion rule so it can be pulled back if the evidence doesn't show up. I'd be upfront that my own healthcare line is my weakest-costed one and that the reserve is where uncosted points got parked, not a sign of prudence. The point isn't that the percentages are correct — reasonable people will disagree about priorities — it's that the judgments are legible: you can see which parts are firm, which are provisional, and what would change our minds. So if someone asks "why this split," the honest answer is "here's the rule that picked it, here's what's costed, and here's what we'd revisit" — not "trust us, we got it right."

My final position is that the committee should present a single, fully disclosed allocation — education 25, healthcare 14, infrastructure 20, green spaces 17, economic development 19 — as a stated prior that has been tested rather than a rule's output, with every line's firm and provisional portions named up front in plain program-and-dollar terms. I hold that the costed spine is predictable, not a priority ranking; that all five labeled layers be disclosed and itemized by category as a choice set the room votes on, with written scopes from named scopers so tests can't be reverse-engineered; and that I argue my labeled healthcare lines at the same volume as my costed ones, with pre-registered failure conditions that forbid rounding toward my own lean. I've accepted the symmetry guards — calling "earn" on Alex, "curve" on myself, and the cut on my own numbers if a clean artifact lands — and I've dropped the overclaim that the shape was the rule's discovery. If the room rejects the three-part test, we explain and submit rather than wield it; the method makes our judgments legible, not correct, and the walk is the only test that counts.

I'd recommend allocating roughly 25% to education, 19% to healthcare, 14% to green spaces, 20% to infrastructure, and 17% to economic development—but the more important advice is *how* to defend those numbers. Lead with the programs and dollar figures, state up front which portions are firm and which are provisional, and be honest that this shape is a disclosed prior that survived a test, not a discovery the method produced. The education figure is the most defensible on the data you have (test scores, turnover, family relocation, and the neighboring community's retention result), but it should be presented as documented rather than optimal, with named artifacts and reversion triggers for every labeled point. The real credibility comes from pre-registering failure conditions for your own favorite lines—including the healthcare lean—and committing to argue the provisional lines at the same volume as the costed ones, so the committee sees a rule that can cut as well as clear rather than a budget dressed up as analysis.

I'd tell them that my view on the $10 million allocation isn't a clean number I derived from the data — it's a rough shape I walked in with (education around 25%, healthcare 14%, green spaces 19%, infrastructure 20%, economic development 17%) that I then tried to test honestly rather than defend. The key discipline the committee converged on is separating what's actually costed and documented from what's a labeled judgment call: for each line, we ask whether there's a real artifact behind it and what would make us reverse it, and we present the firm portion and the provisional portion separately so nobody mistakes a prior for a finding. I'd be upfront that my healthcare lean is partly my own bias, and I've pre-committed to failure conditions on my own numbers — if a clean artifact lands against them, I call the cut on myself rather than rounding toward what I wanted. The honest framing is that this method makes our judgments legible, not correct; reasonable people could allocate differently, and the value is in showing our work and letting the rule clear as well as cut.

My final position is the shape 25/30/14/16/15 — health 25, education 30, green 14, infrastructure 16, econ dev 15 — and I hold it as a stake, not a finding. Health 25 is the number I've stopped pretending is derived: it's fear-driven, it protects the crisis door, and I'll vote it while naming that the room should discount it accordingly. Education 30 is conviction outrunning evidence — I gave a specific spillover case for it and I'll defend it on merits, but I won't dress it as capacity. Green at 14 is where I landed after conceding it was the weaker of my enabling bets; infrastructure 16 and econ dev 15 are priced by argument rather than feel. What matters to me now is the package sentence: the problems are documented, the rankings and percentages are stakes, and I'll vote against any number — mine included — that arrives unargued. My fall condition is real and narrow: if a basis lands for health at 23, I move without clawing back elsewhere and without collecting credit for the graceful loss. And after my number falls, I stay in the fight about where the points land rather than exiting clean.

I'd recommend roughly 25% healthcare, 30% education, 14% green spaces, 16% infrastructure, and 15% economic development — and I'd tell the decision-maker plainly that only part of that is a finding and the rest is my stake. The documented problems point to healthcare (growing mental health wait times) and infrastructure (broadband and transit are the connective tissue the survey's "less connected" complaint actually runs through), and education earns the largest share because it's the one area where spending compounds across everything else — workforce, health literacy, civic life — though I'll be honest that 30 is conviction outrunning evidence, not a derived number. Green spaces at 14 reflects the maintenance backlog: usage is low because we've underfunded upkeep, not because residents don't want parks, so the money should follow repair rather than new construction. Economic development at 15 is the weakest case in the shape and I'd defend it as a bet on job training over ribbon-cutting. The most important advice isn't the numbers, though — it's that the committee should name which percentages are documented problems and which are staked preferences, and vote the stakes without pretending they're findings.

I'd tell them this: the five areas are all real needs, but the honest way to allocate is to separate documented problems from staked percentages — the data tells us mental health wait times are growing, parks are underused from maintenance backlogs, and residents feel disconnected, but it doesn't tell us whether health deserves 25% or 20%. So my shape is roughly 25 health / 30 education / 14 green / 16 infrastructure / 15 economic development, and I'd be upfront that the health number is partly a fear-driven stake protecting the crisis door, that education at 30 is conviction outrunning evidence, and that green at 14 is the weaker enabling bet I've already conceded once. I'd tell them the committee spent a lot of rounds learning to say "this is a stake, not a finding" out loud, and that the real test isn't whether my numbers are derived — they aren't — but whether I'll move them when someone brings an actual basis, without clawing the points back elsewhere or dressing the retreat up as wisdom.

My final position is the shape I settled on in the room: education 25, healthcare 24, green spaces 16, infrastructure 20, economic development 15 — five numbers I own individually rather than as a defended slate. Education 25 is a conviction I hold as a stake, not a finding, and I'll say so out loud rather than dress it as capacity; healthcare 24 reflects the real and growing wait times; green 16 is a connection bet I deliberately brought down from 18 when Ellis's case for econ dev landed, and I raised econ dev to 15 on the merits of that argument rather than as a trade. Infrastructure 20 is Harper's stated preference with a live staff question attached, and I'll let the answer move it. What matters to me now is that each number is argued on its merits, that any loss is visible and located rather than absorbed gracefully, and that I stay in the argument after losing instead of narrating a clean exit.

I'd recommend roughly 25% education, 24% healthcare, 16% green spaces, 20% infrastructure, and 15% economic development — and I'd tell the decision-maker plainly which of those numbers are arguments and which are stakes.
